topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Replicate and rigorously evaluate the compositional generalization failure of the Lewis signaling game on the Shapes synthetic referential game dataset by testing its zero-shot accuracy on unseen attribute combinations within a fixed 48-hour training budget on a single A100 GPU.

BACKGROUND:  
Emergent communication protocols learned by sender-receiver models often achieve high accuracy on training attribute pairs but fail to generalize compositionally to novel object-attribute combinations, limiting their usefulness for scalable multi-agent communication. Prior work (Lazaridou et al., 2018; Andreas, 2019) reports zero-shot accuracy below 80% for the Lewis signaling game on the Shapes dataset, highlighting a key limitation in emergent communication without compositional inductive biases.

APPROACH:  
We implement the standard Lewis signaling sender-receiver architecture with discrete message bottlenecks and train using REINFORCE or Gumbel-Softmax approximations under published hyperparameters (message length ≤ 5, vocabulary ≤ 10 tokens). Training is conducted with early stopping based on plateaued training accuracy (>90%) or zero-shot accuracy stabilization, running 1–2 random seeds within 48 GPU-hours on a single A100. Evaluation focuses on zero-shot accuracy on held-out object-attribute pairs, following splits defined in Lazaridou et al. (2018).

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the publicly available Shapes synthetic referential game dataset (Lazaridou et al., 2018), we measure training accuracy on known attribute pairs and zero-shot accuracy on unseen combinations. The hypothesis is falsified if zero-shot accuracy reaches or exceeds 80% within 48 hours of training. Results are reported as mean ± std over seeds with explicit thresholds and evaluation protocols to ensure reproducibility.

NOVELTY:  
This work formalizes a clear, time- and resource-bounded falsification test of compositional generalization for the Lewis signaling game, providing a reproducible empirical baseline that sharpens previous informal observations. By focusing narrowly on one model, dataset, and a strict evaluation criterion, it sets a standardized benchmark for future compositionality research in emergent communication.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate the compositional generalization capabilities of emergent communication protocols learned via the Obverter Algorithm on the Referential Games Dataset, testing the correlation between sender simulation limitations and generalization performance compared to DRQN and DIAL baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Emergent communication in multi-agent systems often struggles to generalize compositionally to novel attribute combinations, a key challenge for scalable language-like protocols. Prior work (Lazaridou et al., 2017) showed strong in-distribution accuracy for the Obverter Algorithm but did not systematically evaluate its compositional transfer on held-out attribute combinations. Understanding whether the Obverter’s sender simulation constrains generalization is important for designing inductive biases in emergent communication.

APPROACH:  
Train sender-receiver pairs using the original Obverter Algorithm on the Colors and Shapes subsets of the Referential Games Dataset with standard train/test splits that hold out novel attribute combinations. Compare generalization accuracy to baselines using Deep Recurrent Q-Network with Communication (DRQN) and Differentiable Inter-Agent Learning (DIAL) as reported in Foerster et al. (2016). The hypothesis tested is that Obverter’s compositional generalization accuracy will be below 85%, consistent with limitations in sender simulation, whereas DRQN and DIAL may exceed this threshold.

EXPERIMENT:  
Measure communication success accuracy on the in-distribution test set and on a held-out novel attribute combination test set from the Referential Games Dataset (Lazaridou et al., 2017; Andreas, 2019), setting a falsification criterion of ≥85% accuracy on novel combinations. Use identical training conditions for all methods, leveraging publicly available splits and pretrained baselines where possible to conserve compute.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides a focused empirical benchmark of the Obverter Algorithm’s compositional generalization on a canonical dataset, clarifying its limitations relative to established baselines without introducing architectural modifications. It offers foundational quantitative data to guide future research on inductive biases in emergent communication protocols.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether CommNet’s success rate significantly decreases when scaling from 5 to 15 agents on Cooperative Navigation in the Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) under a fixed 48-hour training budget on a single Nvidia A100 GPU, specifically testing if the 15-agent success rate falls below 80% of the 5-agent baseline.

BACKGROUND:  
Emergent communication in multi-agent systems is critical for coordinated behaviors, yet existing benchmarks and architectures like CommNet have primarily been tested on small teams. The scalability of such architectures to larger teams under fixed computational budgets remains an open question, with limited quantitative evidence on how performance degrades with team size in standard benchmarks like Cooperative Navigation in MPE.

APPROACH:  
Implement the original CommNet architecture as described by Sukhbaatar et al. (2016) and train separately on the Cooperative Navigation task with 5 and 15 agents, using identical hyperparameters and reward structures from Lowe et al. (2019). Training runs are limited to 48 hours on a single Nvidia A100 GPU, with early stopping employed if performance plateaus, and evaluation is conducted over 300–500 episodes to estimate success rates efficiently.

EXPERIMENT:  
Measure success rate as the proportion of episodes (out of 300–500) where all agents cover distinct landmarks without collisions within a fixed time horizon. Confirm the hypothesis if the 15-agent success rate is less than 68% (80% of the ~85% success rate reported for 5 agents in Lowe et al., 2019), otherwise falsify it, thereby quantifying performance scaling under fixed compute constraints.

NOVELTY:  
This experiment provides the first rigorous, quantitative evaluation of CommNet’s performance degradation with increased team size on MPE Cooperative Navigation under a fixed training budget, explicitly testing a precise success rate threshold and limiting claims to the tested conditions, thus filling a gap left by prior work that lacks controlled scaling analyses.

topic: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems
text:
IDEA: Evaluate whether incorporating a modular bottleneck with disentangled latent units into Differentiable Inter-Agent Learning (DIAL) improves compositional generalization accuracy on novel object-attribute pairs in the Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) relative to vanilla DIAL.

BACKGROUND: Emergent communication in multi-agent systems often fails to generalize compositionally to novel object-attribute combinations, limiting scalability and flexibility (Foerster et al., 2016; Lazaridou et al., 2018). Prior work shows vanilla DIAL achieves moderate within-distribution success (~50–60%) but drops below 40% on compositional splits in MPE, suggesting a gap in the learned communication protocol’s compositionality. It remains open whether explicit architectural inductive biases can systematically improve this limitation within the DIAL framework.

APPROACH: We implement a simplified modular bottleneck inductive bias in DIAL by factorizing the sender message space into separate embeddings for objects and attributes, using fixed message partitions to encourage modularity without complex disentanglement regularization. The receiver decodes these factorized embeddings jointly to perform actions on compositional inputs. Training follows the original DIAL differentiable communication protocol with standard reinforcement learning, using early stopping based on validation compositional accuracy to ensure reproducibility and resource efficiency.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate compositional generalization accuracy on novel object-attribute pairs using the publicly available MPE dataset and splits from Foerster et al. (2016), comparing the biased DIAL variant to the vanilla baseline (40% accuracy on novel splits) and the Obverter baseline (~75% accuracy on related referential tasks). The hypothesis is falsified if the biased DIAL achieves ≥80% accuracy, with a statistically significant improvement of at least 20 percentage points over vanilla DIAL as a positive supporting result.

NOVELTY: This work rigorously tests a precisely defined architectural inductive bias within the DIAL framework on MPE’s compositional generalization task, improving claim clarity and experimental feasibility over prior broad attributions to inductive biases. By simplifying the modular bottleneck and fixing message partitions, it enhances reproducibility and aligns evaluation directly with established baselines using public datasets and standard metrics.

text:
IDEA: Incorporating pretrained visual-semantic embeddings into the Obverter Algorithm’s receiver model improves compositional generalization accuracy on the ReferItGame Dataset relative to reimplemented RIAL and DIAL baselines.

BACKGROUND: Emergent compositional communication has been demonstrated by the Obverter Algorithm in simple synthetic referential games but has not been tested extensively on complex, visually grounded datasets like ReferItGame (Kazemzadeh et al., 2014). Prior baselines such as RIAL and DIAL (Foerster et al., 2016) have shown effectiveness in multi-agent communication in synthetic environments but lack published results on real-world visual grounding tasks requiring generalization to novel object-attribute pairs.

APPROACH: We adapt the Obverter Algorithm by enhancing its simulated receiver with frozen pretrained visual-semantic embeddings (e.g., CLIP, Radford et al., 2021) to better approximate real-world perceptual complexity. The sender produces discrete messages from a fixed vocabulary (~10 tokens), trained with a two-phase curriculum on known and held-out novel object-attribute pairs. RIAL and DIAL baselines are reimplemented with identical message constraints and training protocols for direct comparison.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate compositional generalization accuracy on held-out novel object-attribute combinations in ReferItGame, using ≥80% accuracy as the threshold for confirming improved compositional communication. Training is constrained to a single NVIDIA A100 GPU per model within 48 hours, with all embeddings pre-extracted to reduce compute.

NOVELTY: This work is the first to apply the Obverter Algorithm with enhanced receiver modeling via pretrained visual-semantic embeddings to a real-world visually grounded dataset, providing a direct comparison to reimplemented RIAL and DIAL baselines on compositional generalization to novel object-attribute pairs with a stringent ≥80% accuracy target not previously reported.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate the impact of nonlinear and asymmetric weight updates in memristor-based synapses on the classification accuracy of a fully-connected spiking neural network trained on the N-MNIST dataset.

BACKGROUND:  
Memristor devices exhibit conductance update non-idealities such as nonlinearity and asymmetry that can degrade the learning accuracy of neuromorphic systems. While prior work (Xu et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021) has characterized device-level synaptic behavior, the precise extent to which these non-idealities impact SNN classification performance on event-based benchmarks like N-MNIST remains underexplored. Quantifying this degradation is crucial for guiding neuromorphic hardware design within realistic constraints.

APPROACH:  
We will implement a fully-connected SNN with one or two hidden layers trained via surrogate gradient descent (Neftci et al., 2019) in PyTorch, incorporating experimentally parameterized nonlinear and asymmetric memristor synapse update rules based on 2TFGM device data (Jeong et al., 2021). Performance will be compared against an ideal linear/symmetric synapse baseline reflecting prior state-of-the-art accuracy (~97%, Lee et al., 2020). Training will be conducted on a stratified subset of N-MNIST to capture representative accuracy trends efficiently within computational constraints.

EXPERIMENT:  
Classification accuracy (%) will be measured on the N-MNIST test set, with the key metric being accuracy degradation relative to the ideal synapse baseline. The hypothesis is falsified if the nonlinear/asymmetric synapse model achieves ≥95% accuracy, indicating minimal impact on learning stability. Validating the hypothesis requires observing ≥5% accuracy drop consistent with prior reported gaps (~7–12%, Xu et al., 2021).

NOVELTY:  
This work provides a reproducible, end-to-end benchmarking study that integrates experimentally measured nonlinear and asymmetric memristor synapse models into modern surrogate gradient-trained SNNs on an event-based dataset, systematically quantifying accuracy degradation without introducing new device characterization or hardware implementation experiments.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Under the evaluated memristor-based synapse model incorporating nonlinear and stochastic weight updates, STDP-trained spiking neural networks (SNNs) on the N-MNIST dataset fail to surpass 90% classification accuracy, indicating that these modeled non-idealities impair learning stability in this context.

BACKGROUND:  
Neuromorphic computing with spiking neural networks (SNNs) aims to emulate brain-like efficiency, but realistic memristive synapses exhibit nonlinear, asymmetric, and stochastic weight update characteristics that may destabilize learning. Prior idealized STDP-trained SNNs achieve ~90% accuracy on N-MNIST (Diehl & Cook, 2015), while backpropagation-trained SNNs reach ~97% (Wu et al., 2018). It remains unclear how memristor device physics constrain functional performance under online plasticity.

APPROACH:  
We simulate an SNN trained with biologically plausible STDP learning on the N-MNIST dataset, explicitly modeling synaptic plasticity with a memristor-based update model adapted from Zhang et al. (2021) and Wang et al. (2020) that includes experimentally characterized nonlinearities, asymmetry, and cycle-to-cycle variability. Controlled comparisons against idealized synapses are conducted using established neuromorphic simulators (e.g., Brian2 or Nengo).

EXPERIMENT:  
We measure classification accuracy on the standard N-MNIST test set after ≤48 GPU hours of training on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. The hypothesis is falsified if accuracy ≥92% is achieved with memristor-modeled synapses, exceeding the 90% baseline from Diehl & Cook (2015), otherwise validated by accuracy ≤90%.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously quantifies the impact of realistic memristive synaptic weight update non-idealities on STDP learning accuracy within a well-established neuromorphic benchmark, bridging device-level constraints with system-level performance. Unlike prior memristor studies focusing on hardware or energy metrics, it precisely tests accuracy degradation in simulation with publicly available datasets and established baselines, providing actionable insights for neuromorphic device design.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
This study quantifies the impact of nonlinear and asymmetric conductance updates observed in ALD HfO2 memristors on classification accuracy of a 5-layer spiking neural network (SNN) trained on the N-MNIST dataset.

BACKGROUND:  
Memristor-based synapses offer energy-efficient hardware implementations for neuromorphic computing, yet device non-idealities such as nonlinear and asymmetric weight updates can adversely affect learning accuracy. Prior high-performing SNN models on N-MNIST achieve ~97% accuracy with ideal synapses, but the influence of realistic memristor update characteristics on accuracy remains empirically underexplored. Understanding this impact is critical to assess the viability of such devices in neuromorphic systems.

APPROACH:  
We implement a 5-layer SNN architecture replicating the model from [1] trained on the publicly available N-MNIST dataset (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.1188975). Synaptic weight updates are simulated using nonlinear, asymmetric conductance change curves extracted from ALD HfO2 memristor data reported in [4], including thresholding and retention effects. A control SNN with ideal linear symmetric synapses as in [2] serves as baseline. Training uses spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) or surrogate gradient methods compatible with both device models.

EXPERIMENT:  
We compare test set classification accuracy, with a falsification threshold defined as surpassing 95% accuracy on N-MNIST using memristor-modeled synapses. Secondary metrics include estimated energy per synaptic operation derived from device switching energy reported in [4].

NOVELTY:  
This work empirically quantifies the performance penalty induced by experimentally measured nonlinear and asymmetric memristive synaptic updates within a rigorously constrained, publicly reproducible neuromorphic learning setup, clarifying their impact relative to ideal synapses and motivating further device-level investigations.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Under a fixed single-layer SNN architecture and identical STDP parameters, nonlinear and asymmetric memristive synaptic weight updates correlate with a greater than 10% classification accuracy drop on the N-MNIST dataset compared to symmetric, linear update models.

BACKGROUND:  
Memristive synapses promise energy-efficient neuromorphic computing but often exhibit nonlinear and asymmetric weight updates that may impair learning. Prior studies (e.g., [2]) report high N-MNIST accuracy (~93%-95%) using symmetric, linear updates, yet quantitative assessments of how realistic nonlinear/asymmetric updates impact classification accuracy under identical STDP protocols remain lacking. Clarifying this impact is crucial for understanding device-level limitations in neuromorphic learning.

APPROACH:  
Implement a spiking neural network with a single hidden layer trained on N-MNIST using standard STDP rules, comparing two memristive synapse models: (1) symmetric linear weight updates modeled after 2TFGM devices ([2]) and (2) experimentally derived nonlinear and asymmetric update characteristics from memristors ([1], [4]). Both models use identical network and training parameters to isolate the effect of update nonlinearity and asymmetry on learning performance.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train both models on a reduced subset (10-20%) of the N-MNIST training data for 5-10 epochs to observe accuracy trends within the 8 GPU × 48-hour compute constraint, then evaluate classification accuracy on the full N-MNIST test set. Confirm the hypothesis if the nonlinear/asymmetric model’s accuracy is more than 10% lower than the symmetric baseline (e.g., if symmetric accuracy is 94%, nonlinear/asymmetric must be <84%).

NOVELTY:  
This study provides the first rigorous, quantitative (>10%) controlled accuracy comparison on N-MNIST between symmetric and nonlinear/asymmetric memristive synapse models using identical STDP protocols and architectures, addressing a critical gap left by prior device-centric or qualitative analyses.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate the classification accuracy limits of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) trained with Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) on CIFAR10-DVS compared to N-MNIST under matched architectures and training regimes, to determine whether BPTT can sufficiently capture complex spatiotemporal dynamics in event-based vision.

BACKGROUND:  
While BPTT-trained SNNs have demonstrated high accuracy on the relatively simple N-MNIST neuromorphic dataset (~92% as reported by Bellec et al., 2018), reported performance on the more complex CIFAR10-DVS dataset remains substantially lower (~60–70%, Amrani et al., 2020). This gap raises open questions about whether BPTT’s temporal credit assignment can generalize to richer event-based data with more complex spatiotemporal patterns, critical for advancing energy-efficient neuromorphic computing.

APPROACH:  
Implement an SNN architecture comparable to Bellec et al. (2018), employing surrogate gradient BPTT with leaky integrate-and-fire neurons unrolled over 20–30 ms temporal windows, trained on both N-MNIST and CIFAR10-DVS while matching hyperparameters and network depth. Computational efficiency will be managed via stratified event subsampling and checkpointing to comply with an 8 GPU × 48-hour resource limit, ensuring reproducibility and alignment with prior baselines.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train and evaluate the SNN on the publicly available N-MNIST [doi:10.3389/fnins.2015.00091] and CIFAR10-DVS [doi:10.1038/s41598-019-44026-0] datasets, measuring top-1 classification accuracy averaged over multiple random seeds and standardized splits. The hypothesis will be falsified if CIFAR10-DVS accuracy reaches or exceeds 85%, demonstrating that BPTT can effectively model complex spatiotemporal features under the tested conditions.

NOVELTY:  
This study critically narrows the scope of BPTT’s generalizability claims by precisely quantifying its performance on complex event-based datasets under controlled, matched experimental conditions, systematically comparing to established N-MNIST baselines. It introduces cost-aware training protocols and a clearly defined falsification threshold to resolve ambiguities in prior literature concerning BPTT’s limitations on diverse neuromorphic vision data.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Quantitatively characterize the correlation between circuit fragmentation and compositional generalization failure in pretrained GPT-2 on SCAN, using targeted activation patching and sparsity metrics to assess modularity limitations underlying systematic generalization deficits.

BACKGROUND:  
Transformer models like GPT-2 systematically fail on compositional generalization benchmarks such as SCAN compositional splits, achieving under 50% accuracy (Wang et al., 2023). It remains unclear whether this failure corresponds to highly fragmented, distributed internal circuits that prevent modular recombination of functional subroutines. Prior work qualitatively suggests fragmented representations but lacks quantitative correlation between circuit structure and behavioral failure modes.

APPROACH:  
Using pretrained GPT-2 small without fine-tuning, we will apply activation patching and sparsity analyses (Nanda et al., 2023; Elhage et al., 2021) on a focused set of SCAN compositional subroutines (e.g., “jump”, “turn left”) to quantify circuit fragmentation and localization. We will compare these metrics to published modularity results from RASP-based transformers that achieve >90% compositional accuracy (Weiss et al., 2021), to characterize how fragmentation relates to GPT-2’s failure.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate GPT-2’s accuracy on SCAN compositional splits, confirming <50% test accuracy; compute fragmentation scores using neuron activation sparsity and patching on targeted examples; contrast with published RASP modularity metrics. The hypothesis is supported if GPT-2 shows high fragmentation (>0.7 normalized sparsity index) correlating with low accuracy, and falsified if accuracy exceeds 90% with evidence of sparse, localized circuits.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides the first quantitative correlation between circuit fragmentation and compositional generalization failure in GPT-2 on SCAN, leveraging targeted mechanistic interpretability techniques to move beyond prior behavioral or qualitative analyses. It sharpens understanding of modularity limitations in standard transformers by grounding failure modes in measurable circuit structure differences relative to modular baselines.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Quantitatively compare circuit modularity, as measured by the Circuit Modularity Score (CMS), between GPT-2 small models trained on WikiText-103 and a synthetic PCFG dataset to establish dataset-dependent differences in circuit entanglement.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability efforts often struggle to identify disentangled circuits within transformer language models, potentially due to overlapping neuron usage across layers. Prior work has noted circuit entanglement but has not systematically examined whether the statistical complexity of natural language corpora like WikiText-103 drives lower modularity compared to structured synthetic datasets. Understanding such dataset-dependent differences is critical for calibrating interpretability expectations and guiding future methods.

APPROACH:  
We will fine-tune GPT-2 small models on both WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017) and the PCFG dataset from BIG-Bench (Srivastava et al., 2022) under matched hyperparameters. Using established mechanistic interpretability techniques—primarily activation patching (Elhage et al., 2021)—we will identify a focused subset (5–10) of linguistically relevant circuits per model and compute their CMS (Nanda et al., 2023), quantifying circuit disentanglement on a 0–1 scale.

EXPERIMENT:  
Circuit Modularity Scores will be averaged over at least 30 identified circuits per dataset, with bootstrapped confidence intervals from multiple random seeds. The falsification threshold is a mean CMS ≥ 0.7 across >80% of WikiText-103 circuits, indicating high modularity despite natural language complexity; CMS < 0.5 would confirm greater entanglement as hypothesized. Results will be interpreted relative to PCFG-trained models’ CMS to isolate dataset effects.

NOVELTY:  
This is the first controlled, quantitative comparison of circuit modularity across natural and synthetic datasets using the CMS metric in transformer models. Unlike prior work that either established patching methods (Elhage et al., 2021) or measured modularity without dataset contrasts (Nanda et al., 2023), this study precisely tests how dataset-induced statistical properties impact circuit disentanglement—providing actionable insights for dataset-aware interpretability research.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Using activation patching on a curated subset of the SQuAD 1.1 dev set, we causally attribute question answering behavior in transformers fine-tuned on SQuAD 1.1 to lexical overlap neuron groups versus candidate multi-hop reasoning neurons identified via HotpotQA, testing whether multi-hop neurons contribute substantially (>70%) during SQuAD QA.

BACKGROUND:  
Transformers fine-tuned on SQuAD 1.1 achieve strong single-hop QA performance (e.g., BERT-base at ~88.5 F1) but are known to over-rely on superficial lexical overlap heuristics rather than genuine reasoning chains, limiting mechanistic interpretability of multi-step inference. Prior work has documented correlational failure modes but lacks causal neuron-level evidence quantifying the relative contribution of lexical overlap versus multi-hop reasoning circuits during SQuAD QA.

APPROACH:  
We fine-tune BERT-base on SQuAD 1.1 and identify candidate multi-hop reasoning neurons via ablation proxies on HotpotQA distractor set. Using activation patching on a ~500-example subset of SQuAD 1.1 dev set focused on challenging examples with low lexical overlap, we swap activations of lexical overlap and multi-hop reasoning neuron groups between correct and incorrect runs. Causal attribution is computed as the proportional drop in accuracy attributable to patching each group.

EXPERIMENT:  
Measure causal attribution percentages of lexical overlap versus multi-hop reasoning neurons on the SQuAD 1.1 dev subset. The hypothesis is falsified if multi-hop reasoning neurons account for >70% of causal attribution on correct SQuAD answers; otherwise, the hypothesis—that lexical overlap neurons dominate—is supported.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides the first causal mechanistic evidence quantifying the relative importance of lexical overlap and multi-hop reasoning neuron groups in transformers fine-tuned on SQuAD 1.1, extending prior correlational analyses by leveraging activation patching at neuron-group granularity on a realistically sized dataset subset under standard compute constraints.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Causally test whether shortcut learning is a significant contributing factor to transformers’ compositional generalization failure on the SCAN benchmark by targeted activation patching and controlled dataset manipulation.

BACKGROUND:  
Transformer models fail to achieve strong compositional generalization on SCAN’s ‘add jump’ split, with vanilla models scoring around 50% accuracy despite their theoretical capacity to represent compositional rules (Lake & Baroni, 2018; Weiss et al., 2021). One leading hypothesis is that this failure stems partly from shortcut learning of spurious correlations in training data rather than inherent representational limitations, but mechanistic causal evidence for this claim remains lacking.

APPROACH:  
Train vanilla Transformers on original and correlation-randomized SCAN splits, then perform mechanistic interpretability analyses focusing on a curated subset of neurons and attention heads identified via lightweight attribution methods as shortcut-related. Use activation patching interventions on this targeted subset during inference to test causal effects on compositional generalization accuracy, combined with automated circuit discovery to validate shortcut versus rule-based circuitry.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate exact match accuracy on the SCAN ‘add jump’ compositional split across standard and shortcut-removed datasets, measuring changes in accuracy after targeted activation patching; surpassing 90% accuracy without explicit shortcut removal would challenge the shortcut learning hypothesis but not fully falsify it. Baselines include published vanilla Transformer accuracy (~50%) and RASP-based transformer accuracy (~95%).

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates causal activation patching with targeted circuit analysis and controlled dataset manipulation to provide mechanistic evidence that shortcut reliance substantially contributes to compositional generalization failure in transformers on SCAN, sharpening prior correlational insights into a testable, causal framework.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Mechanistic disentanglement of overlapping transformer circuits can partially improve compositional generalization accuracy on the SCAN dataset, indicating that entangled representations contribute to failure modes.

BACKGROUND:  
Transformers trained on the SCAN dataset systematically fail to generalize compositionally, achieving below 20% accuracy on key compositional splits such as the "add jump" condition (Lake & Baroni, 2018). Prior mechanistic interpretability work (Nanda et al., 2023; Weiss et al., 2021) suggests that circuit overlap and entanglement impede modular recombination of learned commands, but no study has causally tested whether disentangling these circuits improves generalization.

APPROACH:  
We will identify transformer subnetworks corresponding to primitive commands using targeted activation patching restricted to key layers and heads, then apply post-hoc circuit disentanglement techniques—such as pruning and orthogonalization—without full retraining. The model will be fine-tuned under disentanglement constraints to reduce interference among circuits, aiming to enhance modularity and compositionality.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the SCAN "add jump" compositional split, we measure exact match accuracy to evaluate compositional generalization. Success is defined as improving accuracy from the ~20% baseline to at least 60%, while achieving above 90% would falsify the hypothesis that circuit entanglement is a main limiting factor.

NOVELTY:  
This work provides the first causal investigation linking mechanistic circuit disentanglement to substantial improvements in compositional generalization on SCAN, moving beyond prior circuit identification (Nanda et al., 2023) and training-time interpretability (Weiss et al., 2021) by demonstrating modular recombination benefits without requiring new datasets, architectures, or significantly increased compute.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Quantitatively benchmark Mapper’s clustering concordance with annotated developmental stages in the Mouse Brain Atlas scRNA-seq dataset, contrasting it against persistent homology–enhanced methods and Slingshot to evaluate Mapper’s fragmentation of continuous trajectories.

BACKGROUND:  
Although Mapper is known qualitatively to fragment continuous developmental trajectories in single-cell data, there is a lack of rigorous, quantitative evaluation of this failure mode on real-world datasets such as the Mouse Brain Atlas (Zeisel et al., 2015). Existing trajectory inference methods that integrate persistent homology summaries report higher Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) scores, suggesting better preservation of biological continuity, but direct ARI comparisons with Mapper remain unpublished. This gap limits understanding of Mapper’s practical limitations and parameter robustness on this benchmark.

APPROACH:  
Apply Mapper with standard filter functions (e.g., diffusion maps or PCA) and fixed parameters informed by prior literature to cluster a stratified subsample (∼1,000 cells) of the Mouse Brain Atlas normalized expression data. Compute ARI between Mapper clusters and published broad developmental stage annotations as a proxy for biological coherence. Compare results to PHATE combined with persistent homology feature selection (Moon et al., 2019) and Slingshot (Street et al., 2018) baselines, using published ARIs (~0.7 for PHATE+PH, ~0.65 for Slingshot) for reference.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate clustering concordance via ARI on stratified subsamples to reduce computational overhead, using existing broad cell type annotations from Zeisel et al. as ground truth. Perform persistent homology computations with optimized libraries (Ripser/GUDHI) on the same subsample to ensure feasibility within resource constraints. The hypothesis is falsified if Mapper’s ARI exceeds 0.7, indicating good concordance with developmental stages.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides the first quantitative ARI benchmark explicitly evaluating Mapper’s known fragmentation failure mode on the Mouse Brain Atlas dataset, contextualized alongside topological persistent homology–based and non-topological trajectory inference methods. It clarifies Mapper’s practical clustering performance and robustness without introducing new methods or expanding dataset scope, addressing a current gap in empirical validation.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate the clustering concordance of the Mapper algorithm with default cover parameters on the 10x Genomics PBMC 3k single-cell RNA-seq dataset, demonstrating its sensitivity through ARI scores below 0.7 and motivating parameter tuning for improved biological cluster recovery.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately identifying cell types from high-dimensional scRNA-seq data remains challenging, with topological methods like Mapper offering a promising framework to capture data shape beyond traditional clustering. However, Mapper’s performance critically depends on cover parameter choices, and it is unclear whether default parameters yield clusters that meaningfully correspond to known immune cell types in benchmark datasets such as PBMC 3k.

APPROACH:  
We implement Mapper using KeplerMapper with the first two principal components of normalized gene expression as the filter function and default cover settings (10 intervals, 50% overlap). We measure clustering concordance against annotated cell types via the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), focusing on performance at default parameters and demonstrating sensitivity by limited parameter variation on a representative subset of ~500 cells.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run Mapper clustering on the full PBMC 3k dataset with default cover parameters and compute ARI against established cell labels (Zheng et al. 2017). Perform a reduced sensitivity analysis over a 2×2 grid of cover resolutions and gains on the subset (~500 cells). Compare results to published baseline ARIs for UMAP + Leiden (~0.75) and persistent homology clustering (~0.65) to contextualize Mapper’s cluster recovery quality.

NOVELTY:  
This study precisely quantifies Mapper’s clustering performance under default parameters on a canonical scRNA-seq benchmark, contrasting with prior work that broadly claims topological fidelity without ARI-based validation. By narrowing analysis to clustering concordance and demonstrating parameter sensitivity on a manageable subset, it provides a clear, resource-efficient foundation for future adaptive parameter selection methods.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate the stability of Mapper cluster assignments on a 10,000-cell stratified subsample of the 10x Genomics mouse brain dataset under limited variation of filter functions and cover parameters, quantifying reproducibility via Jaccard similarity across five runs.

BACKGROUND:  
Topological Data Analysis methods like Mapper aim to capture intrinsic data shape in high-dimensional single-cell RNA-seq data, but their stability under parameter changes remains underexplored quantitatively. Existing qualitative reports suggest Mapper’s sensitivity to filter and cover choices may yield inconsistent topological summaries on large-scale datasets such as 10x Genomics. A precise, reproducible assessment of Mapper’s stability on a biologically representative subset is needed to clarify its robustness limitations.

APPROACH:  
Using the KeplerMapper Python library, we will run Mapper on a stratified 10,000-cell subsample of the 10x Genomics 1.3 million mouse brain dataset, varying only the first two PCA components as filter functions and a narrow range of cover parameters (e.g., fixed moderate overlap and interval number). Clusters will be extracted with DBSCAN using fixed parameters tuned in prior scRNA-seq studies. Stability will be quantified by computing pairwise Jaccard similarity of cluster assignments between five independent runs, with cluster label alignment via consensus clustering to ensure valid comparisons.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will measure average Jaccard similarity of cluster assignments across runs, considering values ≤ 0.8 as evidence of Mapper instability on this dataset subset due to parameter sensitivity. This experiment leverages published baselines—UMAP achieving cluster stability ~0.85 (Becht et al., 2019) and persistent homology methods yielding >85% purity on subsets (Guss & Salakhutdinov, 2018)—and is designed to run within 8 GPUs × 48 hours.

NOVELTY:  
This study narrows prior qualitative observations by rigorously quantifying Mapper’s cluster stability on a biologically representative single-cell subsample using a constrained, literature-informed parameter sweep and a carefully justified cluster similarity metric. It sets a practical reproducibility benchmark for Mapper in large-scale scRNA-seq data, guiding future methodological improvements without expanding dataset or method scope.

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate whether adaptive, autoencoder-derived filter functions reduce the variability of Mapper outputs compared to fixed PCA and diffusion map filters on the 10x Genomics 3k PBMC single-cell RNA-seq dataset under fixed cover and clustering parameters.

BACKGROUND:  
Mapper’s topological summaries on high-dimensional scRNA-seq data are sensitive to filter function choice, leading to unstable and non-reproducible cell clustering and trajectory inference (Carrière et al., 2018). While PCA and diffusion maps are commonly used fixed filters, their inability to fully capture nonlinear cell manifold structure may contribute to Mapper output variability. Establishing stable, biologically meaningful topological representations is critical for robust single-cell analysis (Zheng et al., 2017; Nicolau et al., 2011).

APPROACH:  
We will use an autoencoder trained once on the full 10x 3k PBMC dataset to generate a nonlinear, low-dimensional latent embedding whose coordinates serve as adaptive filter functions in the Mapper pipeline (Kingma and Welling, 2013; Lopez et al., 2018). By holding Mapper’s cover and clustering parameters fixed, we isolate the effect of filter function choice, comparing outputs against fixed PCA and diffusion map filters.

EXPERIMENT:  
Stability will be quantified on the 3k PBMC data by performing 30 bootstrap subsamples (80% cells each), computing Mapper graphs with each filter type, and measuring graph variability via Graph Edit Distance (GED) and cluster concordance via Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) of node clusterings. Success is defined as >30% reduction in mean GED and >15% increase in NMI for the adaptive filter relative to PCA filters, consistent with prior stability thresholds (Carrière et al., 2018; Chazal et al., 2014).

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior studies that apply fixed linear or spectral filters, this work evaluates a data-driven, nonlinear autoencoder embedding as an adaptive Mapper filter, rigorously quantifying its impact on output stability while controlling for other Mapper parameters. This addresses a noted gap in systematically improving Mapper reproducibility on well-annotated real scRNA-seq data (Zheng et al., 2017).

topic: Topological methods for high-dimensional data analysis
text:
IDEA:  
Under a standard Mapper configuration using the top 10 PCA components as filter functions and DBSCAN clustering with fixed parameters on 10x Genomics PBMC scRNA-seq data, we evaluate Mapper’s ability to preserve continuous biological trajectories by comparing its pseudotime ordering against published ground truth pseudotime orderings.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately capturing continuous developmental trajectories from high-dimensional single-cell RNA-seq data remains challenging. While topological data analysis methods like Mapper offer intuitive graphical summaries, prior observations suggest that Mapper’s clustering step may fragment intrinsic continuous structures, potentially impairing pseudotime inference. Quantitative benchmarking against robust diffusion-based methods is needed to clarify Mapper’s performance under concrete parameter settings.

APPROACH:  
We apply the Mapper algorithm via the KeplerMapper Python package with PCA-derived filter functions and DBSCAN clustering tuned by k-nearest neighbor distances, constructing Mapper graphs on the 10x Genomics 68k PBMC and 1.3 Million Mouse Brain Cells datasets. Pseudotime is defined as shortest path distances from biologically informed root nodes within the Mapper graph, then correlated (Spearman ρ) with published pseudotime orderings from Monocle 3 and Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT).

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient between Mapper-inferred pseudotime and published ground truth pseudotime on the 10x PBMC dataset, labeling Mapper as failing to preserve trajectories if ρ ≤ 0.6, while baselines (DPT, Monocle 3) are expected to exceed ρ > 0.8, consistent with literature benchmarks.

NOVELTY:  
This work precisely quantifies Mapper’s limitations under standard parameter choices on large-scale, well-annotated 10x Genomics datasets with published pseudotime ground truth, providing rigorously grounded evidence for Mapper’s fragmentation effect and motivating targeted improvements within a narrowly defined experimental scope.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA: Balancing training data during fine-tuning of transformer-based models on the Human Cell Atlas (HCA) immune cell subset reduces downstream cell type classification accuracy disparities between abundant and rare cell types.

BACKGROUND: Foundation models pretrained on single-cell RNA-seq data from the HCA exhibit lower classification accuracy on rare cell types compared to abundant populations, limiting their utility for underrepresented cell populations. Prior studies such as Peng et al. (2022) report a 10–15% drop in accuracy for rare immune cell types using scBERT, suggesting data imbalance as a potential factor.

APPROACH: We will fine-tune publicly available pretrained scBERT models on the HCA immune cell subset, comparing standard imbalanced training to balanced fine-tuning via oversampling or synthetic augmentation of rare cell types. Classification accuracy will be evaluated separately on abundant (>1,000 cells) and rare (<200 cells) populations to quantify the impact of data balancing.

EXPERIMENT: Using the HCA immune cell subset, we measure cell type classification accuracy stratified by abundance after fine-tuning scBERT with and without data balancing. The hypothesis is falsified if the accuracy gap between abundant and rare cell types is reduced to ≤5%. Baselines include published scBERT (~85% abundant accuracy with 10–15% rare accuracy drop) and scVI (~80% balanced accuracy).

NOVELTY: This study explicitly tests the effect of data balancing during fine-tuning on reducing classification disparities between abundant and rare cell types within a transformer-based foundation model, refining previous work by focusing on downstream accuracy metrics without additional pretraining or architectural changes, all within established compute constraints.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether DNABERT’s promoter prediction performance is significantly lower on genomic sequences from underrepresented populations in the 1000 Genomes Project compared to majority populations, using a resource-efficient fine-tuning and evaluation protocol.

BACKGROUND:  
Transformer-based models like DNABERT have shown strong promoter prediction performance (F1 ≥ 0.85) on benchmark datasets predominantly derived from majority populations (e.g., European ancestry in the 1000 Genomes Project). However, population stratification in genomic data may lead to performance disparities when these models are applied to underrepresented populations such as African and East Asian groups. Quantifying this performance gap is critical to understanding the generalizability and limitations of foundation models in genomics.

APPROACH:  
Using publicly available pretrained DNABERT weights, we will fine-tune only the classification head via linear probing on a small, balanced subset (~2,000 sequences) of promoter and non-promoter regions from majority populations (CEU, GBR, FIN). The trained model will then be evaluated without further adaptation on held-out promoter sequences from underrepresented populations (YRI, LWK, CHB, JPT). Baseline performance will be referenced from published F1-scores of Enformer (~0.80) and DeepSEA (~0.75) promoter classifiers; full baseline re-evaluation will be limited to published metrics or small representative subsets to reduce computational overhead.

EXPERIMENT:  
The primary metric is promoter prediction F1-score stratified by population group. The hypothesis is supported if DNABERT’s F1-score on underrepresented populations is at least 10% lower than on majority populations (i.e., drops below 0.77), with baseline models showing less than 5% drop. Evaluation will use promoter annotations from Ensembl Release 104 on sequences extracted from the 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 dataset, constrained to an 8 GPU × 48-hour compute budget.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides a focused, resource-efficient empirical assessment of population-specific generalization gaps in a high-profile genomics foundation model, DNABERT, refining prior broad claims by precisely quantifying performance disparities and framing them without overgeneralization or causal attribution. It leverages publicly available data and state-of-the-art baselines under strict computational constraints to deliver actionable insights on model robustness across diverse human populations.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA: Incorporating orthologous gene grouping into the tokenization of scBERT improves cross-species transfer learning performance between human and mouse immune single-cell RNA-seq datasets.

BACKGROUND: Foundation models like scBERT pretrained on human single-cell RNA-seq data achieve strong clustering performance (ARI ~0.75) on human PBMCs but generalize poorly to mouse immune cells (ARI <0.50), partly due to species-specific gene token vocabularies. Current gene-tokenization schemes do not leverage orthologous gene relationships, limiting the model’s ability to link functionally analogous genes across species in immune contexts.

APPROACH: We re-tokenize input genes by mapping a curated subset of immune-related genes from the human 10x Genomics 68k PBMC dataset and mouse Tabula Muris Senis immune cells to ortholog groups using Ensembl Compara (release 104). Using an existing scBERT checkpoint, we fine-tune the input embeddings and final layers on a ~10k cell subset of human PBMCs with this ortholog-informed vocabulary, then evaluate cross-species transfer by clustering embeddings on a balanced mouse immune cell subset.

EXPERIMENT: Transfer learning performance is measured by Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) on mouse immune single-cell clustering, with improvement of at least +0.10 ARI over standard scBERT (i.e., ARI ≥0.60) considered a positive result; baselines include original scBERT (ARI <0.50) and scVI (ARI ~0.45) on the same datasets.

NOVELTY: This work is the first to explicitly incorporate orthologous gene relationships into the token vocabulary of a single-cell foundation model within a focused immune gene subset, demonstrating biologically grounded vocabulary harmonization that improves cross-species generalization without retraining scBERT from scratch or increasing computational resources.
