IDEA:  
Benchmark the effectiveness of Variational Quantum Error Mitigation (VQEM) on quantum circuits with 10–15 two-qubit gates using Qiskit Aer’s IBMQ Manhattan noise model, quantitatively assessing whether VQEM achieves less than 20% average error reduction under realistic noise conditions.

BACKGROUND:  
Current NISQ devices are limited by noise, and while VQEM has shown promising error reductions (20–40%) on shallow circuits with fewer two-qubit gates (Kandala et al., 2019), its scalability to moderately deeper circuits remains unclear. There is a need to rigorously quantify VQEM’s error mitigation capabilities on circuits closer in complexity to practical QEC codes (e.g., the [[5,1,3]] code) under well-characterized noise models like IBMQ Manhattan, which reflects IBM’s 27-qubit device topology and noise characteristics (IBM Qiskit tutorials, 2019).

APPROACH:  
Using parameterized quantum circuits containing 10–15 two-qubit gates, simulate noisy executions with Qiskit Aer configured with the IBMQ Manhattan noise model. Implement VQEM following Kandala et al.’s variational ansatz and classical optimization (e.g., SPSA or COBYLA), employing resource-aware strategies such as reduced noise sampling during optimization and full noise evaluation post-optimization to remain within an 8 GPU × 48-hour compute budget.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate average circuit error rates (infidelity between ideal and noisy outputs) over 1000 noise instances comparing unmitigated and VQEM-mitigated circuits. Confirm the hypothesis if VQEM reduces errors by less than 20% relative to unmitigated baselines for circuits with ≥10 two-qubit gates under the IBMQ Manhattan noise model.

NOVELTY:  
This study extends prior VQEM evaluations beyond Kandala et al.’s shallow regimes by focusing on moderately deeper circuits with 10–15 two-qubit gates under a realistic, publicly available noise model (IBMQ Manhattan), providing a precise, simulation-based benchmark of VQEM’s scalability limits on NISQ devices rather than physical device demonstrations or idealized noise assumptions.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether confounder-aware methods (FCI, residualization+PC) reduce Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) relative to the vanilla PC Algorithm on the Sachs dataset, providing suggestive evidence that latent confounders contribute to PC’s errors in this specific context.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from observational biological data is challenging due to potential hidden confounders that violate assumptions of standard algorithms like PC. The Sachs et al. (2005) protein signaling dataset, with a known but consensus-based ground truth network, is a benchmark where PC typically yields SHD values above 15 (Kalisch and Bühlmann, 2007), indicating imperfect recovery of causal edges. Understanding whether hidden confounders primarily drive PC’s errors remains an open question.

APPROACH:  
We will compare the Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) of the vanilla PC Algorithm against two confounder-aware variants: (1) the Fast Causal Inference (FCI) algorithm that explicitly models latent confounders, and (2) a preprocessing step that removes latent confounding effects via PCA-based residualization before applying PC. We employ standard Gaussian conditional independence tests within the `pcalg` R package using default parameters to ensure reproducibility and feasibility.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the publicly available Sachs dataset (Sachs et al., 2005; DOI: 10.1126/science.1105809), we measure SHD between inferred and ground truth causal graphs for each method. We confirm the hypothesis if vanilla PC’s SHD remains consistently >15, while FCI or residualization+PC reduce SHD to ≤13, indicating that latent confounders partially degrade PC’s performance on this dataset.

NOVELTY:  
This focused empirical study isolates the impact of confounder modeling on PC’s performance exclusively on the Sachs dataset using well-established baselines and off-the-shelf methods, clarifying latent confounders’ role without extending to new datasets or methods. It explicitly acknowledges ground truth limitations and interprets SHD comparatively, providing precise, testable insights within standard academic resources.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
On bivariate nonlinear cause-effect pairs from the Tübingen Cause-Effect Pairs Dataset, PC Algorithm with nonlinear kernel-based conditional independence tests (KCIT) exhibits significantly lower directional accuracy than NOTEARS, indicating PC’s limitations in capturing nonlinear causal directions in this restricted setting.

BACKGROUND:  
While the PC Algorithm is a classical constraint-based causal discovery method, it commonly struggles with nonlinear dependencies due to limitations of conditional independence tests. NOTEARS, a continuous optimization approach, has demonstrated superior performance on nonlinear synthetic data (Zheng et al., 2018, JMLR) and reportedly outperforms PC by 15-30% SHD on nonlinear pairs in Tübingen (Janzing et al., 2019). However, prior comparisons often rely on linear CI tests, leaving a gap in evaluating PC with nonlinear CI tests on real nonlinear cause-effect pairs.

APPROACH:  
We implement the PC Algorithm enhanced with the nonlinear kernel-based conditional independence test (KCIT) and compare it to NOTEARS using the official codebase (https://github.com/xunzheng/notears). The evaluation focuses specifically on the bivariate nonlinear subset of the Tübingen Cause-Effect Pairs Dataset, testing whether PC’s causal direction classification accuracy is at least 10% worse than NOTEARS. This isolates PC’s nonlinear sensitivity without attributing failure solely to the CI test.

EXPERIMENT:  
We measure directional accuracy (correct causal direction classification) on the nonlinear pairs subset of the Tübingen dataset. Statistical significance and confidence intervals will be estimated via bootstrapping over pairs. Both methods will run within the resource constraint of 8×48 hours on A100 GPUs or equivalent, using efficient implementations and potentially replacing KCIT with computationally cheaper nonlinear CI tests (e.g., RCIT or HSIC-based) to ensure feasibility.

NOVELTY:  
This work sharpens previous PC vs. NOTEARS comparisons by focusing explicitly on bivariate nonlinear cause-effect pairs and using directional accuracy as the primary metric, simplifying evaluation and reducing computational cost. It clarifies PC’s nonlinear detection limitations even when equipped with nonlinear CI tests and does so within a rigorous, reproducible framework leveraging the real-world Tübingen benchmark.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
On the Sachs et al. (2005) Protein Signaling Network dataset, the PC algorithm attains significantly higher Structural Hamming Distance than NOTEARS and TCDF, highlighting limitations of PC’s conditional independence tests in accurately recovering causal edges under the dataset’s conditions, with latent confounders as a plausible contributing factor supported by comparative analysis with the FCI algorithm.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately inferring causal structure from purely observational biological data remains challenging, especially due to latent confounders that can induce spurious dependencies and mislead constraint-based methods like PC. While the PC algorithm is a foundational causal discovery approach, prior literature indicates its sensitivity to hidden variables, but a systematic quantitative evaluation of this limitation on the Sachs et al. dataset against recent continuous optimization and deep learning baselines is lacking.

APPROACH:  
We will apply the standard PC algorithm (using partial correlation tests via the *pcalg* R package), the NOTEARS method (continuous optimization), and the TCDF deep learning approach on the log-transformed and discretized Sachs dataset, evaluating performance by Structural Hamming Distance (SHD) against the Sachs ground truth network. To investigate the role of latent confounding, we will additionally run the FCI algorithm, which accounts for hidden variables, and examine relative SHD differences to contextualize PC’s limitations.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using the Sachs et al. dataset (DOI:10.1126/science.1105809), we will measure SHD for PC, NOTEARS, TCDF, and FCI on identical preprocessed data. The hypothesis is confirmed if PC’s SHD is at least 20% worse than NOTEARS and TCDF (e.g., PC SHD >18 if NOTEARS SHD=15), indicating poorer structural accuracy plausibly linked to latent confounders. Computational costs and preprocessing sensitivities will be explicitly reported to contextualize results.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides the first focused, quantitative comparison of PC’s structural accuracy against modern causal discovery baselines on the Sachs protein signaling data, explicitly examining latent confounder effects via FCI contrasts. Unlike prior work that documents PC’s sensitivity or reports benchmarks separately, our approach quantitatively isolates and contextualizes PC’s limitations in a real-world biological setting without introducing new datasets or methods.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate and quantify the performance degradation of the PC algorithm’s causal graph recovery on ecological time series datasets from CauseMe compared to the Sachs et al. (2005) protein signaling network, highlighting sensitivity to the higher noise and nonstationarity regimes in ecological data.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from observational time series data remains challenging, especially when data exhibit nonstationarity and nonlinear dynamics, as is common in ecological systems. While the PC algorithm achieves approximately 75% accuracy on the relatively stationary Sachs dataset [Kalisch and Bühlmann, 2007], its performance on ecological datasets with greater noise and complex temporal patterns, such as those in CauseMe [Runge et al., 2019], is not well characterized. Understanding these performance differences informs the robustness limits of constraint-based causal discovery methods.

APPROACH:  
Apply the PC algorithm with partial correlation conditional independence tests (via the `pcalg` R package, α=0.01) on both CauseMe ecological time series (Nonlinear Coupled Logistic Maps and Lorenz 96 datasets with ground-truth graphs) and the Sachs protein signaling dataset, standardizing preprocessing and sample sizes where feasible. Compare PC’s normalized Structural Hamming Distance (SHD)-based accuracy across datasets and contextualize results using nonlinear baselines LiNGAM (~60% on linear synthetic data) and TCDF (~85% on nonlinear benchmarks) to benchmark relative robustness.

EXPERIMENT:  
Quantitatively measure graph recovery accuracy by computing normalized SHD against ground truth causal graphs on CauseMe and Sachs datasets. Confirm the hypothesis if PC’s accuracy on CauseMe is at least 20 percentage points lower than on Sachs (e.g., PC ≥75% on Sachs, ≤55% on CauseMe). Repeat with LiNGAM and TCDF to assess if their performance degrades less severely, thereby benchmarking PC’s relative sensitivity to ecological data characteristics.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides a controlled, quantitative benchmark comparing PC’s causal discovery accuracy on ecological versus biological time series datasets, explicitly highlighting a substantial performance gap consistent with the higher noise and nonstationarity of ecological data. Unlike prior work focusing on method development or nonlinear causal discovery, it sharpens understanding of constraint-based methods’ limitations in realistic ecological settings without proposing new algorithms or relying on interventional data.

IDEA:  
On the Sachs Protein Signaling Network Dataset, the PC Algorithm’s precision is below 70%, consistent with potential latent confounder bias, while the FCI algorithm’s explicit modeling of latent variables yields a measurable precision improvement, highlighting the impact of latent confounders on causal discovery accuracy.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery methods like the PC Algorithm rely on conditional independence tests that can be biased by unmeasured latent confounders, potentially degrading graph recovery precision. Although PC is widely used on biological datasets such as Sachs et al. (2005), its limitations under latent confounding remain empirically underquantified, hindering understanding of when and how these confounders impact performance. Addressing this gap is critical for improving causal inference reliability in complex biological systems.

APPROACH:  
We focus on comparing the PC Algorithm and the FCI Algorithm—an extension designed to account for latent confounders—using the Sachs Protein Signaling Network Dataset. Both methods will be run with a standard Gaussian CI test (Fisher’s Z) using default parameters on a reduced subset of proteins known to involve latent confounding. This controlled experimental setup isolates the effect of latent variables on precision without extensive parameter tuning or computational overhead.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate and compare the precision of causal graphs recovered by PC and FCI against the established Sachs ground truth network, using bootstrapped confidence intervals for statistical reliability. The key falsification condition is whether PC’s precision falls below 70%, while FCI achieves precision ≥ 70%, thereby empirically linking latent confounding to PC’s reduced performance.

NOVELTY:  
This work provides the first focused, empirical quantification of latent confounders’ impact on the PC Algorithm’s precision on a real-world biological dataset and demonstrates how FCI’s latent-variable modeling yields tangible improvements. Unlike prior theoretical or synthetic-data studies, it fills a practical knowledge gap by systematically comparing these algorithms on Sachs, clarifying confounding effects in established causal discovery benchmarks.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrate empirical mutation effect features from Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) datasets with precomputed AlphaFold2 confidence metrics (pLDDT and PAE) using lightweight regression models to improve prediction accuracy of mutation-induced protein stability changes without retraining AlphaFold or generating mutant structures.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold2’s predicted Local Distance Difference Test (pLDDT) scores correlate poorly with experimentally measured stability changes upon point mutations, typically yielding Pearson correlations ≤0.2 ([1], [4]). Sequence-based predictors trained on DMS data achieve moderate correlations (~0.3–0.5), but do not leverage structural confidence metrics. There is a need to combine empirical mutation effects and AlphaFold outputs to enhance stability change prediction within proteins with available AlphaFold structures, without incurring the high computational cost of retraining or mutant structure prediction.

APPROACH: Extract AlphaFold2-derived structural confidence features (residue pLDDT, neighborhood pLDDT, predicted aligned error matrices) for wild-type proteins corresponding to mutations characterized in public DMS datasets (MaveDB and SKEMPI 2.0). Combine these with mutation-specific sequence features from DMS data using lightweight machine learning models (e.g., gradient-boosted trees) trained to predict ΔΔG stability changes. The model training will be computationally efficient, requiring only standard CPUs or a single GPU for several hours, and will not modify AlphaFold itself.

EXPERIMENT: Evaluate Pearson correlation between predicted and experimentally measured ΔΔG values on held-out mutations from at least two independent DMS datasets (MaveDB saturation mutagenesis and SKEMPI 2.0). Use AlphaFold pLDDT alone as baseline (~0.1–0.2 correlation [1]) and sequence-only predictors (~0.3–0.5 [1], [4]). The hypothesis is confirmed if combined-feature models achieve Pearson r > 0.3, surpassing pLDDT alone without retraining AlphaFold or generating mutant structures.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that assesses AlphaFold confidence scores in isolation or relies solely on sequence-based predictors, this approach explicitly integrates empirical DMS mutation effect data with structural confidence outputs from AlphaFold without retraining or structural predictions for mutants. This narrow scope improves stability prediction accuracy within proteins with existing AlphaFold structures while respecting realistic computational constraints.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporate interface-sensitive structural features extracted from AlphaFold 3 wild-type complex models combined with side-chain–modeled mutants to improve prediction of binding free energy changes on SKEMPI 2.0 mutations beyond using pLDDT confidence scores alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately predicting the impact of mutations on protein-protein binding affinity remains a challenge despite AlphaFold 3’s advances in complex structure prediction. Prior work shows that AlphaFold 3’s pLDDT confidence scores correlate weakly (∼0.3–0.4 PCC) with experimentally measured ΔΔG values from the SKEMPI 2.0 benchmark (Jankauskaite et al., 2019). This suggests pLDDT alone may insufficiently capture subtle interface rearrangements critical for binding affinity changes.

APPROACH:  
Starting from AlphaFold 3 predicted wild-type complex structures, introduce mutations via side-chain modeling tools (e.g., PyRosetta) without re-running full AF3 predictions, then extract detailed interface features such as residue-level conformational shifts, inter-residue contact distances, and solvent accessibility changes. Train a lightweight regression model combining these features with AF3’s pLDDT scores to predict ΔΔG values on a representative subset (~500–1000) of SKEMPI 2.0 mutations.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate model performance by Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) between predicted and experimental ΔΔG values on the SKEMPI 2.0 subset, aiming to surpass a threshold of ≥0.55 PCC—significantly improving on AF3’s baseline (~0.4 PCC) and MT-TopLap (~0.5 PCC). Use cross-validation ensuring no complex-level data leakage.

NOVELTY:  
This approach explicitly tests whether augmenting AF3 confidence metrics with orthogonal, interface-sensitive structural features extracted from side-chain–modeled mutants improves binding affinity change prediction, refining prior analyses that relied solely on pLDDT. It balances computational feasibility by avoiding full mutant AF3 predictions and narrows scope to a focused, interpretable feature set, providing suggestive evidence on the limitations of pLDDT for mutation impact modeling.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
Integrate AlphaFold2 pLDDT confidence scores with a curated set of biophysically interpretable features extracted from AlphaFold-predicted structures to improve prediction of mutation-induced binding free energy changes (ΔΔG) on the SKEMPI 2.0 dataset, aiming for a Pearson correlation ≥ 0.4 with experimental values.

BACKGROUND:  
While AlphaFold2 achieves remarkable accuracy in protein structure prediction, its residue-wise confidence metric (pLDDT) correlates poorly (r < 0.2) with experimentally measured ΔΔG values for point mutations affecting protein-protein interactions, as shown on the SKEMPI 2.0 benchmark. Existing advanced methods like MT-TopLap improve correlation to ~0.35–0.38 but do not incorporate AlphaFold confidence scores combined with explicit biophysical context. Thus, improving ΔΔG prediction by integrating AlphaFold outputs with interpretable mutation environment features addresses a key limitation in mutation effect modeling.

APPROACH:  
Using publicly available AlphaFold-Multimer predicted structures for a curated non-redundant SKEMPI 2.0 subset, extract pLDDT scores and biophysical features such as solvent accessibility, hydrophobicity, backbone torsions, interface contact potentials, and evolutionary conservation from multiple sequence alignments. Train a simple supervised regression model (e.g., ridge regression) on combined feature vectors to predict ΔΔG values, employing 5-fold cross-validation with complex-level splits to avoid data leakage.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate the Pearson correlation coefficient between predicted and experimental ΔΔG values on SKEMPI 2.0 mutations, validating the hypothesis if the integrated model achieves r ≥ 0.4, outperforming AlphaFold pLDDT alone (<0.2) and MT-TopLap (~0.35–0.38) baselines. Use fixed hyperparameters and publicly available predicted structures to meet compute constraints (≤ 8 A100 GPUs × 48 hours).

NOVELTY:  
This approach demonstrates that combining interpretable, biophysically informed features with AlphaFold2 confidence metrics in a lightweight regression framework can surpass state-of-the-art ΔΔG prediction baselines on SKEMPI 2.0 without retraining AlphaFold or employing complex deep learning architectures, providing a practical and interpretable enhancement over existing mutation effect prediction methods.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating AlphaFold2-predicted wild-type structures and pLDDT confidence scores with a lightweight regression model trained solely on SKEMPI 2.0 mutation ΔΔG data improves the Pearson correlation with experimental ΔΔG values on SKEMPI 2.0 from below 0.3 (baseline pLDDT correlation) to at least 0.5.

BACKGROUND:  
AlphaFold2 (AF2) predicts protein structures with near-experimental accuracy but its confidence metric pLDDT correlates poorly (Pearson r < 0.3) with experimentally measured mutation-induced stability changes (ΔΔG). Existing methods using AF2 complex structures, such as MT-TopLap, achieve correlations up to ~0.45 on SKEMPI 2.0, but predicting ΔΔG reliably remains a major challenge. Improving mutation effect prediction using computationally efficient models leveraging AF2 outputs is an open problem of high practical importance.

APPROACH:  
AF2-predicted wild-type protein complex structures and pLDDT scores will be used to extract local structural and confidence features at mutation sites in SKEMPI 2.0. Mutant features will be generated by modeling residue substitutions on fixed AF2 backbones to avoid costly per-mutant AF2 inference. A lightweight regression model (e.g., gradient boosted trees or small neural networks) trained solely on these features and SKEMPI 2.0 ΔΔG labels will predict mutation ΔΔG values.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using cross-validation on the SKEMPI 2.0 dataset (8338 mutations on 317 complexes), the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) between predicted and experimental ΔΔG values will be computed. Success requires achieving r ≥ 0.5, improving substantially over the baseline pLDDT correlation (~0.2–0.3) and surpassing the top reported value of ~0.45 by MT-TopLap.

NOVELTY:  
This proposes a resource-efficient, interpretable alternative to computationally intensive deep learning models by combining AF2 wild-type structural features with lightweight regression trained on SKEMPI 2.0, demonstrating that substantial improvements in mutation ΔΔG prediction can be achieved without full AF2 mutant structure prediction or large-scale end-to-end model retraining.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating interface conformational ensembles generated from AlphaFold-Multimer predicted complexes improves prediction of protein-protein binding free energy changes (ΔΔG) on SKEMPI 2.0 beyond static structure baselines.

BACKGROUND:  
Predicting binding affinity changes upon mutation remains a major challenge, as AlphaFold-Multimer static complex models correlate modestly (Pearson r ~0.3-0.4) with experimental ΔΔG values on the SKEMPI 2.0 benchmark (Jankauskaite et al., 2019). This suggests that subtle conformational rearrangements at protein interfaces, which influence binding affinity, are not captured by single predicted structures. Existing methods such as MT-TopLap improve this correlation to ~0.5 by integrating structural and topological features but still fall short of high-accuracy prediction.

APPROACH:  
We generate ensembles of interface conformations for each AlphaFold-Multimer predicted complex by applying computationally efficient, knowledge-based conformational sampling focused on mutated residues and their neighbors (e.g., normal mode analysis or limited Rosetta minimization) within resource constraints (8 GPUs × 48 hrs). High-confidence AlphaFold-Multimer models are selected based on pLDDT or interface pTM scores to ensure reliable starting structures. Structural and energetic features averaged over these ensembles are used as input to lightweight regression models (e.g., ridge regression) trained to predict ΔΔG changes.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate Pearson correlation coefficients between predicted and experimental ΔΔG values on held-out mutations in the SKEMPI 2.0 dataset, comparing ensemble-augmented predictions to AlphaFold-Multimer static baselines (~r=0.3-0.4), MT-TopLap (~r=0.5), and Rosetta Flex ddG (~r=0.4-0.5). Demonstrating Pearson r ≥ 0.6 would falsify the hypothesis that interface conformational flexibility alone limits prediction accuracy.

NOVELTY:  
This work narrows prior efforts by explicitly testing the impact of interface conformational ensembles derived from AlphaFold-Multimer structures on ΔΔG prediction accuracy, using computationally efficient sampling and confidence filtering. It thereby rigorously quantifies the added value of dynamic interface modeling beyond static predicted complexes without expanding dataset scope or compute beyond standard academic resources.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA: Under controlled homogeneous system and communication conditions, evaluate how client drift caused by label distribution skew limits FedAvg accuracy on CIFAR-10 non-IID partitions, and investigate knowledge distillation as a complementary mitigation strategy.

BACKGROUND: Federated learning with heterogeneous, non-IID data partitions—such as CIFAR-10 split so each client holds only 2 labels—exhibits accuracy degradation relative to IID baselines (~70%) primarily attributed to client drift (McMahan et al., 2017; Karimireddy et al., 2020). However, prior work has not rigorously isolated client drift from system heterogeneity and communication bottlenecks, leaving ambiguity about their relative impacts on FedAvg’s performance gap.

APPROACH: Implement FedAvg, SCAFFOLD, and FedProx under fully homogeneous simulated system conditions (identical compute, synchronized client updates, no stragglers) on the canonical CIFAR-10 non-IID split to isolate client drift effects. Additionally, augment FedAvg with local-global knowledge distillation at each client to assess whether knowledge transfer regularizes local updates and improves accuracy without altering communication or system assumptions.

EXPERIMENT: Train ResNet-18 models for up to 200 synchronous communication rounds on CIFAR-10 with each client holding data from only 2 labels, evaluating test accuracy as the primary metric. The hypothesis is falsified if FedAvg attains >70% accuracy on this non-IID partition under homogeneous conditions without communication changes; otherwise, persistent accuracy gaps compared to IID baselines confirm client drift as dominant.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior studies (McMahan et al., 2017; Karimireddy et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020) that conflate system heterogeneity or communication factors, this work explicitly controls these variables to isolate client drift’s impact on FedAvg accuracy degradation. Furthermore, it explores local-global knowledge distillation as a novel complementary technique for client drift mitigation in this rigorously controlled federated setting.

IDEA:  
Systematically evaluate whether FedAvg exhibits degraded convergence on the non-IID FEMNIST dataset by comparing its test accuracy against SCAFFOLD under unified experimental conditions to rigorously test the impact of client drift.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning with heterogeneous, non-IID data often suffers from client drift, where local updates diverge due to distinct client data distributions. FedAvg, a standard algorithm, is known to achieve around 70-75% accuracy on FEMNIST but may exhibit unstable convergence due to such drift. Drift mitigation techniques like SCAFFOLD have demonstrated improvements by explicitly correcting for client drift, yet a controlled falsification study isolating FedAvg’s instability under identical conditions remains lacking.

APPROACH:  
We implement FedAvg and SCAFFOLD on the FEMNIST dataset from the LEAF benchmark, using the same CNN architecture, client sampling strategy, and hyperparameters as in their original work without further tuning. Training will run for 50-100 communication rounds with synchronous updates to isolate the effect of client drift on convergence and accuracy, focusing on test accuracy as the key metric.

EXPERIMENT:  
We measure test accuracy on the FEMNIST task with a falsification threshold of 70% for FedAvg: if FedAvg achieves ≥70%, the hypothesis that client drift causes its failure is falsified; if <70%, the hypothesis is supported. SCAFFOLD is expected to exceed FedAvg’s accuracy by at least 5% absolute under these identical settings.

NOVELTY:  
This study uniquely applies a falsification framework under tightly controlled, identical conditions to validate whether FedAvg’s degraded performance on FEMNIST is attributable to client drift, differentiating it from prior benchmarking or algorithm-proposal papers by focusing on rigorous hypothesis testing rather than broad performance comparison.

IDEA:  
Quantitatively measure the correlation between increased variance of local model updates and FedAvg accuracy degradation on the FEMNIST dataset under non-IID splits, highlighting client drift as a significant contributing factor rather than asserting direct causality.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated Averaging (FedAvg) experiences notable accuracy drops (~10-15%) on heterogeneous, non-IID FEMNIST data partitions compared to IID baselines, widely attributed to client drift—divergence in local model updates across clients during training. However, the precise quantitative relationship between local update variance (a proxy for drift) and accuracy degradation remains insufficiently characterized and often overinterpreted as causal.

APPROACH:  
We will focus experiments solely on FedAvg using a reduced subset of 10–20 FEMNIST clients with naturally induced non-IID label skew, running for 20–30 communication rounds. The variance of local model updates \(V_t\) will be computed online per round and summarized without storing full update vectors to minimize overhead. The 20% variance increase threshold for falsification will be anchored against an existing or lightweight IID FedAvg baseline reference.

EXPERIMENT:  
Run FedAvg on FEMNIST non-IID client subsets and compare per-round update variance \(V_t\) and global accuracy against a referenced IID baseline within 30 rounds. Confirm the hypothesis if \(V_t\) increases by at least 20% relative to IID baseline variance and correlates with an accuracy drop of at least 10%. Otherwise, falsify the claim that client drift (measured as update variance increase) is the primary contributor to accuracy degradation.

NOVELTY:  
This study sharpens prior work by rigorously quantifying the statistical association—rather than asserting causality—between local update variance and performance loss in FedAvg, using a computationally efficient experimental setup and an explicit, literature-grounded falsifiability criterion on the well-established FEMNIST benchmark.

IDEA:  
Incorporate adaptive control variates into FedAvg to improve test accuracy on CIFAR-10 non-IID splits by mitigating effects correlated with client drift without increasing communication rounds or payload size.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated Averaging (FedAvg) suffers notable accuracy degradation on CIFAR-10 non-IID partitions, primarily attributed in prior work to client drift, where local models diverge from the global model during training. Existing methods like SCAFFOLD and FedProx mitigate drift but at the cost of additional communication or altered objective functions. Efficiently addressing drift without increasing communication overhead remains an open challenge for heterogeneous federated learning.

APPROACH:  
We propose an adaptive control variate mechanism integrated into FedAvg that dynamically scales variance reduction terms based on local model parameter differences observed during training. Unlike SCAFFOLD, this method estimates and corrects client drift using only standard local update statistics without exchanging auxiliary gradient information, enabling drift correction within the existing FedAvg communication budget.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate on publicly available CIFAR-10 partitioned by label distribution skew (2-3 classes per client) using test accuracy averaged over ≥3 runs. Compare against FedAvg (~68% accuracy baseline), SCAFFOLD (~75%), and FedProx (~73-74%), requiring at least a 5% absolute accuracy improvement over FedAvg without increasing communication rounds or payload per round.

NOVELTY:  
This method differs from prior work by adaptively controlling drift correction without additional communication or proximal terms; it leverages only local model differences for variance reduction, thereby preserving FedAvg’s communication efficiency while empirically improving accuracy consistent with mitigating client drift effects.

IDEA:  
Applying local gradient normalization during FedAvg local updates improves top-1 accuracy by ≥5% over FedAvg on the CIFAR-10 non-IID label distribution skew partition, suggesting a potential reduction in client drift effects without additional control variates or proximal terms.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data commonly suffers from client drift, where local models diverge due to label distribution skew, resulting in degraded global accuracy as shown in McMahan et al. (2017) and Karimireddy et al. (2020). FedAvg accuracy drops from ~75% on IID CIFAR-10 to ~55% on the standard non-IID partition, motivating research into drift mitigation strategies like SCAFFOLD (Karimireddy et al., 2020). However, existing methods introduce complexity or communication overhead, leaving a gap for simpler interventions.

APPROACH:  
We propose incorporating a local gradient normalization (LGN) step in FedAvg’s local training by normalizing gradients at each mini-batch update to unit norm before applying optimizer steps. This lightweight modification requires minimal code changes, does not increase communication costs, and aims to stabilize updates by controlling gradient magnitude variability induced by skewed label distributions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate the LGN-enhanced FedAvg on the CIFAR-10 dataset partitioned non-IID by label as per McMahan et al. (2017), using 20 clients, 30 communication rounds, and local epochs consistent with prior works. Measure top-1 accuracy on the global CIFAR-10 test set, comparing baseline FedAvg (~55%) and SCAFFOLD (~60–65%). Confirm hypothesis if LGN FedAvg achieves ≥60% accuracy, indicating ≥5% absolute improvement.

NOVELTY:  
This work tests a simple, gradient-level normalization technique distinct from prior complex drift mitigation methods like control variates or proximal terms, focusing on accuracy gains within a well-established benchmark. Unlike knowledge distillation or decentralized learning approaches, LGN offers a minimalistic, easily implementable intervention with demonstrated effectiveness specifically on label-skewed non-IID CIFAR-10 partitions.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Evaluate whether a Quantum Variational Classifier (QVC) with a fixed parameterized quantum circuit architecture and encoding scheme fails to match classical Support Vector Machine (SVM) accuracy (~88%) on the Fashion-MNIST dataset within comparable training time, while exhibiting gradient decay patterns consistent with barren plateau phenomena.

BACKGROUND:  
Quantum machine learning promises advantages over classical methods, but barren plateaus—regions of vanishing gradients in variational quantum circuits—may hinder training, particularly on complex, real-world datasets like Fashion-MNIST. Previous work ([Schuld et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.11020)) showed better QVC performance on simpler MNIST data, but it remains unclear whether barren plateaus fundamentally limit performance on more challenging image classification tasks with established classical baselines ([Xiao et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07747)).

APPROACH:  
Implement a QVC using a hardware-efficient ansatz (alternating parameterized single-qubit rotations and entangling CNOT gates) and classical data encoding schemes (e.g., angle or PCA-based encoding) to reduce circuit depth. Train the QVC on a reduced subset and/or downsampled Fashion-MNIST images to fit within an 8 A100 GPU × 48-hour simulation budget using TensorFlow Quantum ([Broughton et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.02989)), monitoring gradient norms primarily during early training to detect barren plateau behavior.

EXPERIMENT:  
Compare QVC classification accuracy on the Fashion-MNIST test set against the classical SVM baseline accuracy of ~88% ([Xiao et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07747)) within the same computational budget. The hypothesis is falsified if QVC accuracy ≥ 88% within training time constraints. Gradient norm decay consistent with barren plateaus will be qualitatively assessed during early epochs.

NOVELTY:  
This study rigorously tests correlations between barren plateau phenomena and QVC underperformance on a realistic, publicly available benchmark dataset with well-characterized classical baselines, under practical computational constraints. It explicitly narrows causal claims and introduces efficient gradient monitoring to identify optimization barriers, advancing empirical understanding beyond prior work focused on simpler datasets or theoretical analysis.

IDEA:  
Under amplitude and angle encoding schemes with PCA-reduced Fashion-MNIST features within current qubit and runtime constraints, Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) fail to achieve ≥90% accuracy on multiclass Fashion-MNIST classification while reproducing ~95% accuracy on binary MNIST (digits 0 vs 1).

BACKGROUND:  
Determining the practical quantum advantage of QSVMs in realistic image classification tasks remains an open problem, particularly as prior work (Rebentrost et al., 2014; Schuld et al., 2019) shows high accuracy (~95%) on binary MNIST but hints at degraded performance on more complex datasets like Fashion-MNIST. The challenge arises from data encoding bottlenecks and increased multiclass complexity, which limit QSVM scalability under current hardware and encoding constraints.

APPROACH:  
Implement QSVMs using Qiskit Machine Learning’s quantum feature maps with fixed hyperparameters and preprocessing (PCA to 64 features) on balanced subsets of MNIST (digits 0 vs 1) and Fashion-MNIST (10 classes), using amplitude or angle encoding circuits up to 8 qubits. Compare against classical SVM baselines from scikit-learn with RBF kernels to benchmark performance under consistent conditions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate test set classification accuracy on (1) binary MNIST subset to reproduce the ~95% baseline from Rebentrost et al. (2014), and (2) a balanced, smaller Fashion-MNIST subset (1,000–2,000 samples) to assess QSVM performance on multiclass classification, with a falsification threshold of ≥90% accuracy on Fashion-MNIST to disprove the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work precisely quantifies QSVM performance limits on multiclass Fashion-MNIST under resource-constrained, fixed-parameter conditions, explicitly linking observed accuracy degradation to encoding and model constraints without overgeneralizing failure causes—providing a grounded, resource-aware empirical boundary for practical quantum advantage beyond prior broader or qualitative studies.

IDEA:  
Empirically evaluate the impact of data encoding schemes on the generative quality of quantum GANs trained on a MNIST subset, testing whether QGANs can match classical DCGAN baselines under practical quantum architectures and resource constraints.

BACKGROUND:  
Quantum generative adversarial networks (QGANs) have been proposed to leverage quantum state expressivity for image generation, but it remains unclear if they can surpass classical GANs on standard benchmarks like MNIST. Prior studies report competitive yet suboptimal Inception Scores (IS) below 8.0 compared to around 9.0 for classical DCGANs, suggesting possible limitations due to the quantum data encoding bottleneck. Clarifying whether current quantum encoding methods practically restrict QGAN performance on MNIST is essential for assessing near-term quantum advantage prospects.

APPROACH:  
We will implement hybrid quantum-classical GAN architectures using TensorFlow Quantum, focusing on two well-studied encoding schemes—amplitude encoding at shallow circuit depth and angle encoding at moderate depth—applied to a representative MNIST subset of 10,000 images. A simplified classical discriminator matching DCGAN design principles will provide adversarial feedback. Hyperparameter tuning will be limited yet literature-informed to maintain feasibility within 8 A100 GPUs and 48 hours of training.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train QGANs on the MNIST subset and evaluate image generation quality using the Inception Score, directly comparing against the classical DCGAN baseline reported at IS ≈ 9.0 (Radford et al., 2016). The hypothesis will be supported if QGAN IS remains below 8.5 despite focused encoding and architecture optimization; falsification occurs if QGANs achieve IS ≥ 9.0, matching classical performance.

NOVELTY:  
This work delivers a targeted, resource-conscious empirical falsification of the data encoding bottleneck hypothesis on MNIST by quantitatively benchmarking QGANs against classical baselines with precise IS thresholds. Unlike prior experimental or theoretical studies, it isolates the encoding impact under constrained circuit depths and encoding schemes, providing actionable insights for near-term quantum generative modeling without expanding dataset scope or methods.

IDEA:  
Evaluate whether quantum kernel classifiers, using standard quantum feature maps and classical data encoding, achieve at least a 5% absolute accuracy improvement over classical kernel methods on the MNIST dataset, without attributing performance differences solely to encoding bottlenecks.

BACKGROUND:  
Quantum kernel methods have been proposed as a promising approach for quantum machine learning, with potential advantages in expressivity and generalization. However, classical data encoding schemes may limit the feature space accessible to quantum kernels, and prior empirical results on MNIST suggest quantum methods do not substantially outperform classical kernels. It remains an open question whether quantum kernels can demonstrate a clear accuracy advantage under experimentally feasible encoding and training settings.

APPROACH:  
We systematically compare quantum kernel classifiers built with standard quantum feature maps and classical encoding schemes against classical kernel classifiers on MNIST. The study restricts data preprocessing and hyperparameter tuning to feasible scales to preserve computational tractability. Results are interpreted in terms of accuracy performance gaps without inferring causality beyond the observed metrics.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train and evaluate quantum kernel classifiers and classical kernel baselines on a downscaled MNIST subset using classification accuracy. The falsification criterion is that quantum kernel accuracy on MNIST must exceed classical kernel accuracy by at least 5 percentage points to disprove the null claim of no meaningful quantum advantage.

NOVELTY:  
This work sharpens the inquiry into quantum kernel performance by focusing strictly on measurable accuracy comparisons under realistic resource constraints and explicitly acknowledging confounding factors beyond classical data encoding, differentiating it from prior studies that over-attribute performance limitations.

IDEA:  
Precisely evaluate whether Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) using low-depth quantum feature maps can outperform classical Support Vector Machines (SVMs) with RBF kernels by at least a 3% accuracy margin on binary classification subsets of MNIST.

BACKGROUND:  
While prior work (Havlíček et al., Nature 2019; Schuld & Killoran, PRL 2019) has shown QSVMs achieve comparable accuracy (~95-97%) to classical RBF SVMs (~98%) on MNIST binary subsets such as digits {3,5} and {4,9}, no statistically significant advantage has been demonstrated. The open question is whether current quantum feature maps provide sufficient expressivity to surpass classical kernel methods on these standard benchmarks.

APPROACH:  
We restrict claims specifically to the tested MNIST binary subsets and the known low-depth quantum feature maps from Havlíček et al. (2019). QSVMs will be implemented via Quantum Kernel Estimation circuits simulated using PennyLane or Qiskit with GPU acceleration, while classical SVMs with RBF kernels will be trained using scikit-learn with limited hyperparameter tuning based on published baselines. Dataset sizes and splits will be downsampled to ~500 training and ~200 test samples per class to reduce computational load without sacrificing the ability to detect a ≥3% accuracy difference.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using identical, publicly available MNIST binary classification splits for {3,5} and {4,9}, we will measure held-out test accuracy for both QSVM and classical RBF SVM models. The hypothesis that QSVMs outperform classical SVMs will be falsified if QSVM accuracy exceeds classical by at least 3% with statistical significance confirmed via confidence intervals or hypothesis testing.

NOVELTY:  
This study sharpens prior qualitative comparisons by enforcing a precise, quantitative falsification criterion (≥3% accuracy margin) on established MNIST benchmarks using existing quantum feature maps, while improving resource efficiency through dataset downsampling and bounded hyperparameter tuning. This focused, reproducible design provides clearer evidence on the limits of current QSVM expressivity relative to classical RBF kernels.
